paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: X-ray diffraction is a general name for what happens when X-ray beams change direction after interacting with the electrons around atoms. It comes from elastic scattering, in which the energy of the waves does not change. Far from the sample, the directions the X-rays take can be mapped, and that map is called a diffraction pattern.

paragraphs.heading: Waves from every electron
paragraphs.text: A crystal is a regular array of atoms, and X-rays are electromagnetic waves. Atoms scatter those waves, mainly through their electrons. Picture an ocean wave hitting a lighthouse: secondary circular waves spread out from the lighthouse. In the same way, an X-ray that strikes an electron sends secondary spherical waves out from that electron. A regular array of scatterers gives a regular array of spherical waves. In most directions these waves cancel one another, which is called destructive interference, but in a few specific directions they add together.

paragraphs.heading: Bragg's picture of sheets
paragraphs.text: The Bragg model gives an intuitive way to understand this. In it, a given reflection is tied to a set of evenly spaced sheets that run through the crystal, usually through the centers of its atoms. William Lawrence Bragg proposed that incoming X-rays are scattered from each plane the way a mirror reflects. X-rays from neighbouring planes then add together when θ, the angle the X-ray makes with the plane, gives a path-length difference that is a whole-number multiple n of the X-ray wavelength λ.

paragraphs.heading: The puzzle of what X-rays were
paragraphs.text: Wilhelm Röntgen discovered X-rays in 1895. At the time physicists were unsure what X-rays were, though they suspected waves of electromagnetic radiation. Single-slit experiments in Arnold Sommerfeld's laboratory suggested a wavelength of about 1 angstrom. X-rays also had particle-like properties, such as ionizing gases, and in 1907 these led William Henry Bragg to argue that X-rays were not electromagnetic radiation. His view proved unpopular. In 1912 Max von Laue observed X-ray diffraction, and that confirmed X-rays are a form of electromagnetic radiation.

paragraphs.heading: The 1912 experiment
paragraphs.text: The idea that a crystal could serve as a diffraction grating for X-rays came up in 1912, when Paul Peter Ewald and Max von Laue talked in the English Garden in Munich. Ewald had a resonator model of crystals that could not be checked with visible light, because the wavelength was much larger than the gaps between the resonators. Von Laue saw the need for electromagnetic radiation with a shorter wavelength, and he proposed X-rays, whose wavelength might be comparable to the spacing in crystals. With Walter Friedrich and Paul Knipping, he shone an X-ray beam through a copper sulfate crystal and recorded the diffraction pattern on a photographic plate. The developed plate showed rings of fuzzy, roughly elliptical spots. The image was crude and unclear, yet it confirmed the diffraction concept.

paragraphs.heading: Laws and Nobel Prizes
paragraphs.text: Laue developed a law that ties the scattering angles to how large the unit-cell spacings in the crystal are and how they are oriented. For it he received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1914. The field then grew quickly, most notably through William Lawrence Bragg and his father William Henry Bragg. The younger Bragg developed Bragg's law in 1912–1913; it links the scattering to evenly spaced planes inside a crystal. For their work in crystallography, the two Braggs shared the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1915.
